heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background, 1.2 Restatement of the problem)
note: One background paragraph, one routing paragraph, five restated tasks. 29 is context with no figures: countries compete on comprehensive strength, higher education reflects science and technology, a healthy system supplies talent - the only evidence offered is the observation that developed countries attract international students. 30 states the remit (build a standard, build models, propose and analyse a policy suite) and glues the '1.2 Restatment of the problem' heading into its tail, so the problem statement is one sentence. 31-40 restate the five ICM-F tasks, split two printed lines per block, and the restatement is faithful and unusually precise for this corpus: crosswise contrast model, apply it to several countries and pick one with room for improvement, a realisable vision, vertical contrast model for current and proposed systems, targeted policies with an implementation schedule plus policy-effectiveness evaluation, and the practical impact of the transition. Note that the paper's summary text appears twice - identically in blocks 3-8 (the summary sheet) and again in 14-19 (the body's own summary page) - so the front matter alone consumes fourteen measured blocks for six paragraphs, and the TOC (20-28) ends by gluing the '1 Introduction / 1.1 Background' headings into block 28's tail.

heading: 2 General Assumption
note: Four assumptions, each split one printed line per block, so every group is one paragraph. 1 (41-43): the number of higher education institutions is stable, because founding a university takes long. 2 (44-48): a unified standard for defining government education expenditure exists across countries, which is the assumption that makes the Expenditure index comparable and is stated as a requirement rather than a fact ('it is necessary to unify the standards'). 3 (49-53): the collected statistics are reliable, with the sources named inside the assumption - ARWU [1], Ranking Web of Universities [2], Project Atlas [3] - a good practice that appears nowhere else in the paper. 4 (54-56): the selected nations have stable political, social and economic environments and suffer no earthquake, war, economic crisis or terrorism, and 56's tail glues the '3 Symbol Table / Symbol / Meaning / xij' header. Assumption 4 is what licenses the linear-summation model: with no shocks, a score built from five normalised indices is stable, and the paper's own weakness section names exactly this as a limit. Nothing in the chapter says how the government-expenditure standard is unified, which leaves the Expenditure index - the one India scores highest on - the least comparable of the five.

heading: 3 Symbol Table
note: The symbol table as seventeen measured blocks, coded as one group because the measurement split the two-column table cell by cell - the interleaving is visible inside the blocks ('Expenditure on tertiary education (% of government expenditure on 微信号：MATHmodels EXP1 [4] education) [5] EXP2' holds four cells and two citation markers). It declares x_ij (country i's value on index j), y_ij (index j at time i) and the inputs behind the five indices: EXP1 and EXP2 (tertiary expenditure as a share of education expenditure, and total education expenditure as a share of government expenditure), FMR1 and FMR2, ENL, INB, TOPN, UNI, and the six ARWU sub-indicators (Alumni, Award, HiCi, N&S, PUB, PCP - with 'Staﬀof' for Staff and 'Nature and Science∗' carrying a stray asterisk). Three defects: the table contains no weights and no index levels for the composite, so the notation cannot express the score the paper computes; the ARWU sub-indicators are declared although RES is defined only as TOPN/UNI, so six declared symbols are never used; and block 73's tail glues the '4 Models' heading. The count of inputs is also unstable across the paper - 14 factors here and in the summary, 13 parameters in the strengths section (block 227).

heading: 4 Models (4.1 Detailed indices: Exenditure, Enrolment, Gender equity, Research level, Internationalization)
note: Five indices, one formula each, and the whole model is these five ratios. 74 states the health criteria - national attention and government investment, popularisation, academic achievement, international recognition, no sexual discrimination - and reduces them to three dimensions (cost and capital, access and equity, academic level). 75 announces the 14 factors and points at Figure 1. Then, index by index: Expenditure EXP = EXP1 x EXP2 (76, with definitions in 77 and justification in 78); Enrolment ENI = ENL (78, 79, 80); Gender equity GEI = 1 - FRM1/FRM2 (80-82, formula split at the block boundary); Research level RES = TOPN/UNI (83, 84, with the 194-word justification in 85 citing ARWU and the two ARWU figures in 86-87); Internationalization INT = INB/UNI (88-90, where 88's block holds both the Figure 3 caption and the formula). Three structural defects and one sign error. The sign error: GEI = 1 - FRM1/FRM2 gives ZERO when female-to-male enrolment equals the national female-to-male ratio, i.e. the index scores perfect gender balance as 0, and block 82 explicitly says a healthy system has balanced enrolment - so the index is inverted relative to its own definition (as printed; the extraction's layout of (3) makes FRM1/FRM2 the only reading). The structural defects: (a) section 4.1.3 has no heading at all - the numbering jumps 4.1.2, [nothing], 4.1.4, 4.1.5, so the gender index is introduced inside block 80 as an unlabelled formula; (b) RES = TOPN/UNI and INT = INB/UNI share a denominator, so any policy that reduces UNI raises BOTH indices with no change in research output or in foreign students - and the paper's own vision 4 (blocks 141-143) halves the number of universities, which mechanically doubles two of the three indices it calls shortcomings; (c) EXP = EXP1 x EXP2 is a product of two percentages, so a country spending a large share on education and a large share of that on tertiary education scores multiplicatively, giving a range that is not on the same scale as the other four indices, and no normalisation to a common scale is described in this chapter. Block 90's tail glues the '4.2 Using TOPSIS-like algorithm / 4.2.1 Crosswise contrast model' headings.

heading: 4.2 Using TOPSIS-like algorithm (4.2.1 Crosswise contrast model, 4.2.2 Vertical contrast model)
note: Two models that are the same model with a different matrix. Crosswise (91-97): build X = (x_ij) of countries by indices (92), standardise by vector norm z_ij = x_ij / sqrt(sum_i x_ij^2) (94, cited to [12] - a 简书 blog post), write Z (95), score s_ij = z_ij x 20 (96), total S_i = sum_j s_ij (97). Vertical (98-104): build Y = (y_ij) with time instead of country (99), same standardisation (101, same [12] citation), same Z (102), same s_ij = z_ij x 20 (103), same S_i (104). So the 'TOPSIS-like algorithm' contains no ideal solution, no anti-ideal solution, no distance measure and no weights - it is a norm normalisation followed by an equal-weight sum, and the 20 multiplier merely rescales each index to a nominal maximum of 20 so the total tops out at 100. Three consequences the paper does not state: the scores are purely relative to the sample (a country's score depends on which other countries are in the matrix, so 'Australia 53.8' is not a statement about Australia); the five indices are equally weighted with no justification, although the chapter 4 text argues each measures a different dimension; and the two matrices reuse the same symbol Z and the same variables z_ij and s_ij across equations (13) and (14) for a completely different meaning, so the notation cannot distinguish a country score from a year score.

heading: 5 Select a higher education system with room for improvement
note: Five blocks, and the selection decision that the whole rest of the paper rests on. 106 reports the five countries (Australia, India, Japan, Sweden, United Kingdom), the reference year (2017) and points at Figure 4. 108, a 294-word block, gives the scores - Australia 53.8, India 23.29, Japan 23.54, Sweden 48.13, Britain 49.01 - and then reads them: gender balance is similar across all five, Australia is 'relatively perfect' with high scores everywhere, and the sentence is cut mid-way and resumes in 109 ('for sustainable development'), whose tail glues the '6 A concrete analysis of India's higher education system' heading. The decisive arithmetic: India is chosen because it is lowest, but it is lower than Japan by 0.25 points out of 100 - a margin smaller than the rounding of the printed values in the same sentence (23.29 and 23.54), on a score built from one normalised sample of five countries. No uncertainty, no second sample, no robustness check on the ranking appears anywhere in the paper; the sensitivity analysis in chapter 7 perturbs indicator values by 5% and 10% but only reports that the response is linear, so it does not test whether India and Japan can be separated. The paper also names the same country 'United Kingdom' (106) and 'Britain' (108), and 108 mixes it with Sweden in the ordering (48.13 for Sweden, 49.01 for Britain) without a table - the numbers are only in the figure the reader cannot check against the text.

heading: 6 A concrete analysis of India's higher education system (6.1 Problems, 6.2 Vision and vision assessment)
note: India's diagnosis, then a vision set as four numeric targets, then the vision scored. 110-111 compare India's five scores with the best score achieved by any of the five countries (Figure 5); 112 (233 words) diagnoses: India has the HIGHEST Expenditure index but a research index far below the others, 'which suggests that the ratio of education investment to academic output is seriously inconsistent' - the sharpest inference in the paper, and it is a statement about the same multiplicative EXP index whose scale was never made comparable; 113 completes the sentence and glues the 6.2 and 6.2.1 headings. 114 states the vision: ENI, RES and INT are the shortcomings, so four five-year plans over twenty years (2017 to 2037) target those three. The four targets are where the paper's numbers actually live. Target 1 (115-125): 70% of Indians are low-caste or 'untouchable' (an unsourced figure - the 2011 census puts Scheduled Castes at 16.6% and Scheduled Tribes at 8.6% of the population, so 70% only works if Other Backward Classes are folded in, which the text does not say), the top 30% are to reach Australia's 113% gross enrolment, the rest k x 113% with k = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, giving an expected rate of (0.3 + 0.7k) x 113% - arithmetic correct, rising 41.8% to 65.5%. Target 2 (126-134): 5, 8, 9 and 7 new universities entering the ARWU top 500 in successive five-year blocks, with the argument that growth is faster early then decelerates - an asserted schedule with no base count, so the implied RES cannot be computed, and the target is stated for a country whose own vision 4 then halves the number of universities. Target 3 (135-140): inbound foreign students up 7% a year for five years, then 11%, then about 5%. Target 4 (141-143): reduce the number of universities by 50% in the first five years by abolishing or restructuring. 144 is Figure 6, the implementation schedule. 145-148 score the vision: predicted data into the vertical contrast model, scores rising every five years through 2037 (146), with Figures 7 (per-index) and 8 (total), and 148's tail glues '6.3 Policy proposal'. The vision section is the paper's most concrete part and also its most circular: targets 1-3 are set as percentages, and target 4 divides the denominator of two of the three indices the vision is supposed to fix, so the improvement in RES and INT is partly definitional.

heading: 6.3 Policy proposal (6.3.1 promote enrolment, 6.3.2 improve HEIs, 6.3.3 internationalization)
note: Three policy blocks, each built the same way - a mechanism paragraph, a routing sentence, then a numbered list - and every item split one printed line per block. 6.3.1 enrolment (149-158): the mechanism is the caste system and the rich-poor gap, with the caveat that India's tertiary share of education spending is already high but badly allocated (151); three policies - a more progressive tax system, redistributing per-student funding toward poor students, and mixing public with private investment (153-158). 6.3.2 institutions (159-182): the mechanism is the teacher shortage - high entry thresholds, weak incentives, rigid tenure, an 'outrage' evaluation and training system (160) - and five policies: abolish the bottom 30% of universities, merge the middle 40% two-into-one and keep the top 30%, halving the total (162-167); give institutions financial, academic and management autonomy with transparent allocation (168-171); create an independent National Research Foundation to cut red tape (172-175, cited [15]); train domestic teachers and import foreign ones (176-180); overhaul the curriculum around 'core essentials' and experiential learning (181-182). 6.3.3 internationalization (183-196): the mechanism is weak faculty and low attraction (183), then six policies - legislation and scholarships, international courses and faculty, better urban and campus facilities, publicity, twinning programmes with simpler visas, and attracting top-100 universities to open Indian campuses under a new law (184-196). Two observations. The strategies are concrete and costed in institutional terms, which is rare in this corpus, but only the university-merger policy is tied to a model quantity (the RES and INT denominators) and the tax and funding policies have no modelled effect at all - the vertical contrast model has no fiscal variable, so 6.4's claim that policy improves the score is not connected to these instruments. And the merger policy is stated twice with different numbers: vision 4 says cut the number by 50% by abolishing or restructuring (141-143), while 6.3.2 achieves the same 50% by abolishing 30%, merging 40% into 20%, and keeping 30%.

heading: 6.4 Policy effectiveness evaluation, 6.5 The practical influence and difficulty of implementing the plan
note: The effectiveness claim and the impact discussion. 197-198 read the vertical-contrast result: with the high expenditure and gender scores maintained, enrolment, top-500 share and international students all rise, so 'the implementation of the policy is effective' - but the evaluation does not run the policies through the model; it runs the vision's targets (the predicted indicator values set in 6.2) through it, so the result restates the assumptions of the targets rather than testing the instruments of 6.3. 198's tail glues the '6.5' heading. 199-200 set up the chain-effect discussion. Four impacts follow, all argued rather than modelled: the caste system, because education was 'a status stabiliser rather than an invader on status rigidities' (201-206, and note block 203 carries a broken citation marker '[?]', the only place in the paper where a source is invoked but not supplied); the tax system, since equal taxation violates fair redistribution and the plan taxes the middle and upper classes more (207-210); the education system, streamlined by support for poor students, private investment, mergers and teacher training (211-218); and international influence (219-221). 222, a 180-word block, admits the plan will be hard to implement because the policies offend the interests of the established groups, and its tail glues the '7 Sensitivity analysis' heading. The discussion is the paper's most honest chapter - it names the political losers - and it also exposes the gap the model cannot cross: none of these four impacts is measurable in the five indices, so the paper's own framework cannot register the effects it spends the chapter describing.

heading: 7 Sensitivity analysis
note: One 58-word paragraph is the entire sensitivity analysis: each of the five indicators was changed by 5% and 10%, a new score was computed, and the result is 'a linear relationship between the scores and figures of indicators', with the total score also responding linearly. Two things follow. First, the finding is a tautology: the model is s_ij = 20 x_ij / sqrt(sum x^2), so a common scaling of an indicator changes the score by a known algebraic factor with no interaction between indices - there is nothing else a perturbation could show. Second, and more seriously, the perturbation that matters is not tested: whether the India-Japan gap of 0.25 points (108) survives a change in the sample of countries, since the norm normalisation makes every score depend on the other four countries in the matrix. Changing one indicator by 5-10% within a fixed five-country matrix cannot answer that. The chapter has no table, no numbers and no figure, and it is followed immediately by the strengths chapter, so the paper's robustness claim rests on a single sentence.

heading: 8 Strength and weakness of the models (8.1 Strength, 8.2 Weakness)
note: Four strengths and three weaknesses, every bullet split one printed line per block, and the labels run on: each strength's heading sits in the tail of the previous strength's last block (229, 232, 234, 238), so the measurement cannot separate labels from content. Strengths: inclusive, five independent indicators from 13 parameters (227-229 - note the count, 13 here against 14 in the summary and in block 75); quantified, so evaluation is 'clearer and more intuitive' (230-232); simple but universal (233-234); and comparative, since 'score of one education system is meaningless unless the score is obtained by comparison' (235-238) - which is the paper's clearest statement of its own relativism and, read against block 108, also its main vulnerability, because a 0.25-point gap in a purely relative score is being used to select a country. Weaknesses: accuracy depends on the statistics (239-240); some parameters are subjective (241-243); and natural disasters and human disruptive events are excluded (244-245, whose tail glues the 'References' heading). The three admissions are real but none of them names the problems this reader can verify - the inverted gender-equity formula, the shared UNI denominator, the missing 4.1.3 heading, or the 70% low-caste figure. References follow at 246-272 (seventeen entries, mostly data URLs: ARWU, Webometrics, Project Atlas, six World Bank indicators, plus a 简书 blog as [12]); Appendix A follows at 272-276 and contains only four figure captions - 'Crosswise contrast model: raw data input', 'data after standardization', and the same pair for the vertical model (273-276) - so the raw data and the standardised matrices that every score depends on are images, not numbers, and cannot be checked from the text.
